strengths: NC-OOD offers a useful, simple post-hoc detector. Reusing classifier weights and a global feature mean avoids storing training-feature banks or performing nearest-neighbor searches, giving a plausible practical advantage with little additional computation.

The evaluation covers CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, two architecture families, and cross-entropy and supervised contrastive training. Table 1 reports mean AUROC of 95.36 on CIFAR-10 and 94.15 on ImageNet, exceeding the evaluated baselines. Under contrastive training, Table 8 improves mean FPR95 from KNN+'s 11.61 to 9.84.

The component ablations provide meaningful evidence for combining alignment and magnitude. On ImageNet, the full score achieves 94.15 AUROC versus 88.69 for pScore and 87.08 for the L1 norm alone (Table 4). Comparisons with alternative similarity metrics further support the chosen score.
The scoring rule and geometric motivation are clearly explained. Selecting the combination weight using Gaussian-noise validation avoids requiring examples from the evaluated natural OOD datasets.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is not established under its stated assumptions. Equation (3) controls normalized error, whereas Equation (1) asserts absolute convergence. With zero within-class variability, a class-mean radius growing as t and angular misalignment decreasing as t^(-1/2) satisfy NC1 and NC3 while the absolute error grows as sqrt(t). Additional assumptions are needed. The angular motivation remains plausible, but the manuscript also lacks quantitative collapse diagnostics connecting its trained models to the limiting assumptions.

The specific contribution beyond existing scoring ideas is insufficiently isolated. pScore is the predicted-class linear response after feature centering and normalization, combined with an already established feature-norm signal. A matched comparison using empirical class means instead of classifier weights would clarify the benefit of the proposed construction. Relevant efficient baselines such as ViM and ASH are also absent, weakening the state-of-the-art positioning for CVPR 2025.

The evidence supports competitive average AUROC more strongly than consistent superiority across scenarios. On DenseNet/CIFAR-100, NC-OOD has FPR95 of 62.62 versus KNN's 47.36 (Table 10), and its mean AUROC is below DICE+ReAct (86.18 versus 86.79). ImageNet FPR95 essentially ties DICE+ReAct (27.28 versus 27.25). These qualifications matter for the central versatility claim, although they do not erase the improvements elsewhere.

Several reporting discrepancies affect comparative interpretation. Table 10 reports ReAct+DICE's mean FPR95 as 76.45, but its six listed values average approximately 45.00. Section 4.4 claims that pScore outperforms KNN on every ImageNet OOD dataset, yet Texture AUROC is 91.86 for pScore versus 97.07 for KNN. These are substantive inconsistencies beyond presentation refinements.

Experimental reliability and reproducibility remain incomplete: the manuscript does not specify the supervised-contrastive classifier-head training procedure, KNN's k and sampling settings, or an exact ImageNet checkpoint identifier. No repeated-run uncertainty establishes the stability of the modest average gains, and latency/memory measurements do not substantiate the efficiency claims. Together with the theoretical and comparative gaps, these reservations balance the useful practical contribution at the decision boundary.
